title: The old way
hookLine: elderly brahmins ask whether their people still live the way the ancient sages did

cards: Lots of families keep a founder story. Great-grandparents who arrived with one suitcase and worked six days a week and never wasted bread. Companies have them too: two people in a garage.
So do schools and congregations. And sooner or later someone asks the uncomfortable question: are we still like that?

A group of elderly brahmins from Kosala, wealthy and well respected, come to the Buddha with exactly that question about their own people. Do the brahmins of today live by the ways of the brahmins of old?

teach.h: NO CATTLE, NO GOLD: LEARNING WAS WEALTH
teach.b: The Buddha answers gently, and mostly with praise for the past. The sages of old, he says, were self-controlled and austere. They had no cattle, no gold, no stored grain.
Learning was their wealth, and they guarded it like treasure. Food was set out for them at doors, given with trust. Nobody turned them away.
They spent their youth in study and pure living.
When they made offerings, they offered rice, bedding, clothes, butter and oil, and no cow was killed.
Cows, the poem says, were like mothers and fathers and brothers to them, friends who gave food, strength, beauty and ease. Then the poem tells a story of change.

teach.h: THE SPLENDOR OF KINGS, AND DRIFT
teach.b: In time, those sages saw the splendor of kings: fine clothes, chariots, beautiful houses. Desire for that life crept in. Sacrifices grew grand and costly, and animals began to be killed at them.

And the poem says that when the knife fell on the cow, the gods themselves cried out that it was wrong. The elders who asked the question are moved, and they take refuge. Notice how the Buddha answers.
The poem is sharp about the drift, but he doesn't scold the men in front of him.

He answers their question with their own ancestors, and holds up a picture any tradition, any family, anyone might recognize: a simple beginning, slowly filled with comfort and display, and elders brave enough to ask.
In this poem, simplicity and self-control aren't a new teaching. They're the old one.

how: Buddhist monastics live on alms and own very little, and lay Buddhists often take extra precepts on observance days to practice simplicity, such as eating before noon and setting aside entertainment and adornment.

o: the ancient ones, the sages of old
a royal sacrifice of great cost
the newest teachings of the day

games.q: the old way: tap the pairs.
p: desire for the splendor of kings

s: the elders who ask the question are brahmins themselves
wealthy, elderly brahmins from Kosala ask about their own tradition.
the poem says the ancient sages killed animals at their offerings
it says they offered rice, butter, oil and cloth, and no cow was killed.
at the end the elders leave angry
they are moved and take refuge.

games.q: you're one of the elders. the Buddha has described the ancient sages and how things drifted. what do you do?
o: praise the teaching and take refuge.
games.why: the elders are moved by the picture of the old way and go for refuge.

practice: Think back to when you first started something that mattered, a friendship, a job, a faith, a hobby, and remember what it was like before it filled up with extras.
Breathe with that beginning for a moment: the thing itself, without the gear, the audience or the upgrades.

wordCard.voice: Porana, the ancient ones. The Buddha's picture, for elders who asked, of the simple, self-controlled life of the ancient sages, and of how easily anyone drifts from it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali porana: ancient, of old. the poem speaks of the porana brahmana, the brahmins of old.

carryVoice: Your line: plainly, without extras. The beginning is still there underneath. Day five hundred ninety-seven.
